title: Cheongung-II Suppliers: Who Makes the Radar, Launcher and Missile Behind $9.5 Billion in Exports
content:
South Korea's Cheongung-II (KM-SAM Block II) air defense system has export contracts with three Middle East countries worth about $9.5 billion combined: about $3.5 billion with the UAE, about $3.2 billion with Saudi Arabia and about $2.8 billion with Iraq. The multi-function radar is made by Hanwha Systems, the launcher and launch tubes by Hanwha Aerospace, and the missile, engagement control and system integration by LIG Nex1 (renamed LIG Defense & Aerospace in April 2026). Its local content was reported at about 95% as of July 2025.

1. Three export contracts, about $9.5 billion

The UAE signed in January 2022 in Dubai for about $3.5 billion, with Tawazun, the UAE's defense procurement body, as the counterparty. Saudi Arabia's deal of about $3.2 billion was signed in November 2023 and disclosed in February 2024. Iraq signed on September 19, 2024 in Baghdad for about $2.8 billion, or roughly KRW 3.7135 trillion. All three figures are rounded, and a combined won total is not given because exchange rates differ by contract date. The UAE system is deployed and operating; the Saudi and Iraqi contracts are being carried out.

2. How the launch differs from Patriot

Patriot fires with the motor ignited inside the launch tube, so the launcher must be turned toward the target. Cheongung-II uses a cold launch: gas pushes the missile more than 10 meters straight up, and it ignites in the air.

The order of turning in the air and then igniting follows an Asia Economy report of March 14, 2026. All-round 360-degree coverage comes from vertical launch and an initial turn, not from cold launch itself, and the missile still produces flame after igniting. It has not been established that cold launch caused the export wins.

3. The radar: Hanwha Systems

The radar that acts as the system's eyes is made by Hanwha Systems. One radar handles detection, tracking and friend-or-foe identification, and export units were reported at about $1.1 billion in total.

4. The launcher and tubes: Hanwha Aerospace

Hanwha Aerospace makes the launcher and launch tubes. A launcher contract between Hanwha Aerospace and LIG Nex1 was reported at KRW 940 billion (Newdaily, December 26, 2024). At the time of the UAE deal the company was named Hanwha Defense, which Hanwha Aerospace absorbed in November 2022.

5. The missile and engagement control: LIG Nex1

LIG Nex1 handles system integration, final missile assembly and the engagement control station. Its name changed to LIG Defense & Aerospace after a March 31, 2026 shareholder vote and an April 14 relisting; it is the same company. A battery consists of six missile launch vehicles, a multi-function radar and an engagement control station.

What could and could not be confirmed

Confirmed: contract sizes and dates for the three exports, who makes each part, and the Hanwha Defense merger date. Not confirmed: the roughly 96% interception rate reported for UAE-deployed batteries comes from a lawmaker's statement cited in news reports (about 60 interceptors fired, March 2026), and no original UAE or Korean government data, counting period or success criteria were found. It is a different figure from the 100% hit rate in development test firings announced by Korea's defense procurement agency. The 95% local content figure is from a Korea Economic Daily report of July 6, 2025; the claim that the remaining 5% is non-core parts could not be re-confirmed in the original. Hanwha contract values come from reports citing filings, not the filings themselves. Cheongung and Cheongung-II are different systems; the exported one began development in 2012 and was handed to the military in November 2020.

Quick FAQ

How much are the Cheongung-II exports worth?
About $3.5 billion (UAE), $3.2 billion (Saudi Arabia) and $2.8 billion (Iraq), about $9.5 billion combined. All are rounded figures.

Who makes the Cheongung-II radar?
Hanwha Systems makes the multi-function radar, which detects, tracks and identifies targets.

Why does LIG Nex1 appear under another name?
It was renamed LIG Defense & Aerospace and relisted on April 14, 2026. It is the same company.

Is the 96% interception rate an official figure?
No. It comes from news reports citing a lawmaker's statement, and original government data was not found.

Companies named are disclosed or reported suppliers; amounts are rounded. Images are reconstructions based on public information, not actual footage. Sources include the Korean defense procurement agency's Cheongung-II delivery release, the Ministry of National Defense release of February 7, 2024 (Saudi contract), Maeil Shinmun and Seoul Shinmun (Iraq, September 20, 2024), Korea Policy Briefing (cold launch), Asia Economy (March 14, 2026), Electronic Times (March 12, 2026), Newdaily (December 26, 2024), Korea Economic Daily (July 6, 2025) and U.S. CRS IF13299 (Patriot).
